meta.title: The manager and management accounting
meta.summary: How management and cost accounting differ from financial accounting, strategy and the value chain, the five-step decision process, guidelines for management accountants, where cost accounting came from, and professional ethics.

videos.title: Financial, management and cost accounting
videos.take: Management accounting serves managers inside the firm; cost accounting measures the costs they need

scenes.say: Financial accounting tells outsiders how a company did. Management accounting helps the people inside run it. Here's the difference.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of accounting
scenes.say: Financial accounting reports to investors and lenders, follows GAAP and looks back at the whole company. Management accounting serves managers, follows no required rules, looks forward, and drills down into products, jobs and departments.

sub: costs, for both kinds of accounting
scenes.say: Cost accounting sits between the two. It measures, analyzes and reports the costs of acquiring and using resources. Inventory and cost of goods sold for the financial statements come from it, and so do the product costs managers use to price and plan.

sub: built to order in Marshall, Minnesota
scenes.say: Meet the company we'll follow this semester: Prairie Gate Trailers, which builds custom livestock and utility trailers to order in Marshall, Minnesota. Its owner, Karen Olsen, needs to know what each trailer really costs.

scenes.heading: Questions Karen asks
items: What did trailer #418 cost to build?
Should we bid $14,000 on a new order?
Why was welding over budget last month?
scenes.say: Karen's questions are management accounting questions. What did a particular trailer cost? What price should she bid? Why was a department over budget? None of these appear in the annual report.

scenes.q: Which question is a management accounting question?
opts: What was net income under GAAP?
Which trailer model is most profitable?
How should the bank loan be classified?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which is a management accounting question? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Product profitability is an internal decision question. The others are financial reporting.

videos.title: Strategy and the value chain
videos.take: Cost information supports strategy across every business function in the value chain

scenes.say: A company competes either by being cheaper or by being different. Cost accounting supports both strategies. Here's how.

scenes.heading: Two broad strategies
scenes.say: A cost leader wins by having the lowest costs, like a maker of standard utility trailers. A differentiator wins by offering something customers value and will pay more for, like a custom trailer for show cattle. Prairie Gate does a bit of both.

scenes.heading: The value chain
scenes.say: The value chain is the sequence of business functions that make a product valuable to customers: research and development, design, production, marketing, distribution and customer service. Costs arise in every one of them, not only in the factory.

scenes.heading: Key success factors
scenes.say: Customers judge a company on a handful of key success factors: cost, quality, time, innovation and, increasingly, sustainability. Management accountants track all five.

The supply chain stretches outside the company: from steel and axle suppliers, through Prairie Gate, to dealers and the farmers who buy the trailers. Cutting costs often means working with partners along it.

scenes.q: Prairie Gate's warranty repairs fall in which value chain function?
scenes.say: Quick check. Prairie Gate's warranty repairs belong to which value chain function? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's D, customer service. Costs after the sale are part of the value chain too.

videos.title: The five-step decision process
videos.take: Managers identify, gather, predict, decide, then implement and evaluate; planning and control link them

scenes.say: Good decisions follow a pattern. Management accountants help at every step. Here's the five-step process.

scenes.heading: Five steps
scenes.say: First, identify the problem and the uncertainties. Second, obtain information. Third, make predictions about the future. Fourth, choose among alternatives. Fifth, implement the decision, evaluate performance and learn.

scenes.heading: Should Prairie Gate add a stock-trailer line?
scenes.say: Karen wonders whether to add a line of standard stock trailers. Sales expects a hundred and twenty a year at $9,500 each. Cost accounting predicts $7,800 of cost per trailer. That's $204,000 of margin a year, before any new fixed costs.

scenes.heading: Planning and control
scenes.say: Steps one to four are planning: choosing goals and how to reach them, summed up in a budget. Step five is control: comparing what happened with the plan in performance reports, then learning.
Feedback closes the loop. If actual costs come in higher than predicted, next year's predictions improve.

scenes.q: Comparing June's actual welding costs with the budget is part of which step?
scenes.say: Quick check. Comparing June's actual welding costs with the budget is part of which step? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's D. Evaluating performance against the plan is control, step five.

videos.title: Guidelines and the controller
videos.take: Use cost–benefit thinking, consider behavior, and remember different costs for different purposes

scenes.say: Three guidelines run through this whole course. And the person who usually applies them is the controller.

scenes.heading: Three guidelines
items: Cost–benefit: is the information worth what it costs?
Behavior matters: systems change how people act
scenes.say: First, cost–benefit: better information is worth having only if its benefits exceed its cost. Second, systems shape behavior: how you measure people changes what they do. Third, different costs for different purposes: there's no single right cost for a product.

scenes.heading: Trailer #418: different costs, different purposes
scenes.say: For the balance sheet, trailer four-eighteen's cost includes only factory costs. To price a repeat order, Karen needs all value chain costs, including design and delivery. To decide on a one-off special order, only the extra costs matter.

scenes.heading: Who does what
scenes.say: In most companies, the controller is the chief management accountant, responsible for cost systems, budgets and reporting. The treasurer handles cash and financing. Both report to the chief financial officer.
Accountants are usually staff, not line managers. Production managers make the decisions; accountants supply the analysis that helps them decide well.

scenes.q: Karen considers buying a $40,000 costing system that will save $10,000 a year for 2 years. Which guideline does she apply?
scenes.say: Quick check. Karen considers a forty thousand dollar costing system that saves ten thousand a year for two years. Which guideline applies? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Benefits of $20,000 don't justify $40,000 of cost.

videos.title: Where cost accounting came from
videos.take: Cost accounting grew from factory owners, railroads and engineers, and was reinvented in the 1980s

scenes.say: Cost accounting wasn't invented by a standard-setter. It grew out of factories, railroads and arguments about profit. Here's the short history.

scenes.heading: Milestones
scenes.say: In the 1770s, the potter Josiah Wedgwood analyzed his costs to survive a slump. In the 1850s, American railroads tracked cost per ton-mile. Engineers inspired by Frederick Taylor developed standard costs in the early twentieth century. DuPont formalized return on investment around 1914.

sub: Costing showed which wares lost money
and how volume cut unit cost
scenes.say: Wedgwood's costing in 1772 showed him which wares lost money and that unit costs fell as volume rose. Those are still core ideas: product costing and fixed costs spread over output.

sub: costing had fallen behind the factory
scenes.say: By the 1980s, critics said cost systems were built for financial reporting, not decisions. Johnson and Kaplan's 1987 book, Relevance Lost, argued management accounting had stalled. Its answer, activity-based costing, is Lecture 6.
The lesson: costing systems reflect the businesses of their time. Labor-heavy factories allocated overhead by labor hours. Automated factories needed something better.

scenes.q: What problem did Relevance Lost (1987) highlight?
opts: Cost systems driven by financial reporting, poor for decisions
scenes.say: Quick check. What problem did Relevance Lost highlight? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Product costs built for external reporting misled managers making decisions.

videos.title: Professional ethics
videos.take: The IMA's standards are competence, confidentiality, integrity and credibility
videos.read: IMA Statement of Ethical Professional Practice

scenes.say: Management accountants are often under pressure to make the numbers look better. Professional ethics tells them what to do.

scenes.heading: IMA overarching principles
scenes.say: The Institute of Management Accountants, which awards the C-M-A credential, sets out four overarching principles: honesty, fairness, objectivity and responsibility.

scenes.heading: Four standards
scenes.say: And four standards: competence, keeping your skills up; confidentiality, protecting information; integrity, avoiding conflicts of interest; and credibility, reporting information fairly and completely, including bad news.

Suppose Prairie Gate's plant manager, whose bonus depends on profit, asks the accountant to delay writing off scrapped steel until next year. That would misstate results: a credibility and integrity problem.

scenes.heading: Resolving an ethical conflict
items: Discuss with your supervisor, or higher
scenes.say: The IMA's advice: follow the organization's policies; discuss the issue with your supervisor, or the next level up if the supervisor is involved; get confidential advice, for example from an IMA ethics counselor; and consult a lawyer about your rights and obligations.

scenes.q: An accountant shares Prairie Gate's bid prices with a friend at a rival firm. Which standard is broken?
scenes.say: Quick check. An accountant shares Prairie Gate's bid prices with a friend at a rival. Which standard is broken? Pause and pick.

warmup: Think of a business you've worked in. What cost number did your manager care about most, and was it in the annual report?
Common answers: labor cost per shift, food cost percentage, cost per delivery. Almost none appear in external reports. Leads to 1.1.
acts: Classify each report as financial or management accounting: (a) cost per trailer by model, (b) 10-K, (c) monthly scrap report, (d) audited balance sheet.
Place each Prairie Gate cost in the value chain: CAD software license, steel, trade-show booth, delivery truck fuel, warranty labor.
Design; production; marketing; distribution; customer service.
Apply the five steps to Prairie Gate's question: should it buy a robotic welder?
Identify (labor shortage, quality); obtain info (quotes, labor rates); predict (savings, volume); decide (compare with hiring); implement and evaluate (track weld defects and cost).
Give three different 'costs' of trailer #418 for three different purposes.
Inventory cost (factory only); full value-chain cost for long-run pricing; incremental cost for a one-off decision.
Why did labor-hour overhead allocation make sense in 1920 but mislead in 1985?
In 1920 labor drove most overhead; by 1985 machines and complexity did, so labor bases distorted product costs.
The plant manager asks you to delay the scrap write-off. Walk through the IMA steps.
Refuse to misstate; follow policy; raise with supervisor (above the plant manager if needed); seek confidential advice; document; consult counsel if pressured.
case: Prairie Gate's plant manager, Dale Kirchner, earns a bonus if 2026 operating income exceeds $900,000. In mid-December, forecasts show $880,000. Dale asks the cost accountant, Priya, to (1) delay recording $25,000 of scrapped steel until January, and (2) record a trailer finished on January 3 as completed in December. Priya reports to Dale, who reports to Karen Olsen.
Which IMA standards are at stake?
What would the two changes do to 2026 income?
How could Karen redesign the bonus to reduce this pressure?

Integrity and credibility. Both shift income into 2026, misstating it by about $25,000 plus the trailer's margin. Priya should refuse, follow policy, take it to Karen since Dale is involved, seek confidential advice, and document. Redesign: multi-year or non-financial measures, ranges instead of cliffs.
exam: Distinguish financial accounting, management accounting and cost accounting.
Financial: external users, GAAP, historical, aggregate. Management: internal, no required rules, future-oriented, detailed. Cost: measures and reports costs used by both.
Explain 'different costs for different purposes' with an example.
No single correct cost: inventory valuation uses manufacturing costs; long-run pricing uses full value-chain costs; special orders use incremental costs.
outcomes: Distinguish financial, management and cost accounting
Link cost information to strategy and the value chain
Apply the three guidelines and describe the controller's role
Outline the history of cost accounting
take: Management accounting looks forward, inside the firm
Costs arise across the whole value chain
Plan with steps 1–4, control with step 5
Cost–benefit, behavior, different costs for different purposes
Costing systems reflect the businesses of their time

ex.why: Management accounting serves internal decisions; financial accounting serves outsiders under GAAP.

ex.q: Put the value chain in order.
ex.why: The value chain runs from R&D to after-sale service.

ex.q: Match each cost to its value chain function.
Put the decision steps in order.
ex.why: Steps 1–4 are planning; step 5 is control.

ex.q: A new line sells 80 trailers a year at $9,000; predicted cost is $7,500 each. What is the predicted annual margin before new fixed costs?
Who is usually the chief management accountant?
ex.why: The controller runs costing, budgeting and reporting.

ex.q: Match the action to the IMA standard it violates.
ex.why: These are the IMA's four standards.
